title_original: Hoor Al Qasimi Appointed Curator of the 62nd Venice Biennale

blocks.text: A transformative force in contemporary art, Hoor Al Qasimi brings to Venice a curatorial vision that has consistently challenged established cultural hierarchies, championed artistic practices across the Global South and reshaped the geography of the international art world.
Suzette Bell-Roberts

La Biennale di Venezia has announced the appointment of Hoor Al Qasimi as curator of its 62nd International Art Exhibition, to be held in 2028. The appointment recognises one of the most esteemed curators and institution-builders working today, whose achievements over more than two decades have challenged the historical concentration of cultural authority within Europe and North America. Hoor Al Qasimi, Artistic Director of the 25th Biennale of Sydney, Rememory (2026), photographed at White Bay Power Station, Sydney, Australia, 2025. Photograph: Daniel Boud. Courtesy of the Biennale of Sydney.

blocks.caption: Hoor Al Qasimi, Artistic Director of the 25th Biennale of Sydney, Rememory (2026), photographed at White Bay Power Station, Sydney, Australia, 2025. Photograph: Daniel Boud. Courtesy of the Biennale of Sydney.

blocks.text: Al Qasimi’s commitment extends beyond increasing the visibility of artists from historically marginalised regions to establishing the institutional conditions through which their practices can be supported, researched, contextualised and understood on their own terms. Her work has been instrumental in shifting contemporary art’s focus towards the Global South, recognising its diverse artistic traditions, intellectual histories, and knowledge systems as central to international cultural discourse.

Among her most consequential achievements is her transformation of the Sharjah Biennial. Having co-curated its sixth edition in 2003, Al Qasimi has remained its Director, overseeing its evolution from a predominantly regional exhibition into one of the world’s most critically engaged and internationally respected biennials. Under her leadership, successive generations of curators have had the intellectual freedom and institutional support to interrogate dominant art histories, explore alternative modernities, and establish meaningful connections across geographical and cultural boundaries.

In 2009, Al Qasimi founded Sharjah Art Foundation, extending her vision beyond the biennial to establish a year-round cultural programme. Integral to her approach is a commitment to preserving Sharjah’s cultural and architectural heritage through the restoration and adaptive reuse of historic and modern buildings, transforming them into spaces for contemporary art, research and community engagement. Her vision demonstrates how inherited cultural knowledge can serve as a foundation for innovation and artistic production.

Rather than positioning the Global South in relation to established Western centres, Al Qasimi has cultivated relationships across Africa, Asia, the Middle East, Latin America and their diasporas, facilitating artistic and intellectual exchanges that transcend conventional geopolitical divisions. Opening ceremony of the sixth Aichi Triennale, A Time Between Ashes and Roses , Japan, 2025. Courtesy of Sharjah Art Foundation.

blocks.caption: Opening ceremony of the sixth Aichi Triennale, A Time Between Ashes and Roses , Japan, 2025. Courtesy of Sharjah Art Foundation.

blocks.text: Her appointment to Venice follows a distinguished trajectory of curating major international biennials and triennials. In 2015, she curated the United Arab Emirates National Pavilion at the 56th Venice Biennale, presenting 1980 – Today: Exhibitions in the United Arab Emirates , which examined the country’s contemporary art history.

She subsequently curated the second Lahore Biennale, Between the Sun and the Moon (2020), exploring the interconnected histories and cultural relationships of South and West Asia. In 2023, she realised the 15th Sharjah Biennial, Thinking Historically in the Present , conceived by the late Okwui Enwezor, examining the enduring legacies of colonialism and foregrounding artistic practices that offer alternative readings of history.

As Artistic Director of the sixth Aichi Triennale in Japan, A Time Between Ashes and Roses (2025), Al Qasimi addressed humanity’s relationship with the natural world, ecological fragility and collective responsibility. Her curatorial vision for the 25th Biennale of Sydney, Rememory (2026), explored the relationship between memory, history and identity, foregrounding lived experiences frequently excluded from dominant historical narratives.

Collectively, these exhibitions demonstrate her ability to develop curatorial frameworks responsive to particular geographical, historical and cultural contexts while recognising the interconnected nature of contemporary global realities.
Announcing the appointment, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, President of La Biennale di Venezia, stated:

“Throughout her career, Hoor Al Qasimi has succeeded in creating a caravanserai of geographies and the Universal, giving voice to stories and sensibilities shaped by research and the unexpected. Her work brings together a profound attentiveness to deep-rooted memory and its legacies, an open perspective on the intricate complexities of the present, and a rare ability to listen to places and their people.” Hoor Al Qasimi.Photograph: Chieska Fortune Smith. Courtesy of Sharjah Art Foundation.

blocks.caption: Hoor Al Qasimi.Photograph: Chieska Fortune Smith. Courtesy of Sharjah Art Foundation.

blocks.text: Reflecting on her appointment, Al Qasimi recalled her first encounter with the Venice Biennale:

“The International Art Exhibition of La Biennale di Venezia has been an important platform for many of us around the world. I first visited the 50th edition in 2003, shortly after stepping into my curatorial role at Sharjah Biennial. For me, La Biennale remains a critical space to engage with the work of influential artists and curators.

“I am honoured to have been invited to curate this exhibition and grateful to President, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, and the board for their confidence and trust. I look forward to working with the team of La Biennale and welcoming audiences to the 62nd edition.”

Beyond exhibition-making, Al Qasimi’s leadership of The Africa Institute, Sharjah’s Global Studies University, the Sharjah Architecture Triennial and the International Biennial Association reflects her commitment to building sustainable cultural and intellectual infrastructure. These institutional endeavours recognise the interdependence of artistic practice, education, architecture, historical research and knowledge production.

In recognition of her outstanding contribution to contemporary art and international cultural exchange, France awarded Al Qasimi the insignia of Officier de l’Ordre des Arts et des Lettres (Officer of the Order of Arts and Letters) in 2025. She was also appointed Ambassador Extraordinary for Arab Culture for 2025–2026 by the Arab League Educational, Cultural and Scientific Organisation (ALECSO). H.E. Nicolas Niemtchinow, Ambassador of France to the UAE, Hoor Al Qasimi, President and Director of Sharjah Art Foundation and Stéphanie Salha, Advisor for Cooperation and Cultural Action of the Embassy of France in the UAE and Director of the Institut Français in the UAE, during the decoration award ceremony at The Flying Saucer, Sharjah. blocks.text: Following Koyo Kouoh’s In Minor Keys , Al Qasimi’s appointment is particularly significant. Both curators have dedicated their careers to questioning the assumed universality of Western art histories and establishing platforms through which artists can articulate their own intellectual traditions, histories and contemporary realities. Their successive appointments recognise curatorial perspectives that have long challenged the established hierarchies of the international art world.

For ART AFRICA , having worked with Sharjah Art Foundation for more than fifteen years, this announcement is particularly welcome. Al Qasimi’s achievements demonstrate what sustained institutional commitment can accomplish beyond the temporary visibility afforded by international exhibitions. Her work has strengthened artistic ecosystems, recovered overlooked histories and established new centres of intellectual and creative exchange.

The significance of her appointment lies not simply in the prospect of broader representation at Venice, but in the possibility of reconsidering the perspectives from which contemporary art and its histories are understood. Al Qasimi brings to Venice an exceptional record of translating curatorial conviction into institutional action. Her achievements affirm the Global South not as a territory awaiting recognition from established cultural centres, but as a vital force shaping the intellectual and artistic direction of contemporary art.
